table.title: Security advisories for affected dependencies
table.html:
CVE IDPackageAffected versionsSeveritySummary
CVE-2024-6387OpenSSH (sshd)>=8.5p1 <9.8p1CriticalA signal handler race condition in sshd can be triggered by an unauthenticated remote client during authentication, leading to memory corruption and potentially unauthenticated remote code execution as root on glibc-based Linux systems. Exploitation is timing-dependent but has been demonstrated in controlled environments; administrators should upgrade to 9.8p1 or apply the vendor backport and restrict exposure of SSH services where possible.
CVE-2023-44487nghttp2>=1.0.0 <1.57.0HighThe HTTP/2 protocol implementation permits a client to open many streams and immediately reset them, causing the server to allocate and release request state faster than it can be reclaimed. This rapid reset pattern can exhaust CPU and memory and degrade or deny service to legitimate clients; the fix introduces stream concurrency limits and faster cleanup of canceled streams.
CVE-2024-21538cross-spawn>=6.0.0 <6.0.6, >=7.0.0 <7.0.5HighInefficient regular expression handling in the command parsing logic allows an attacker who controls part of a spawned command string to cause catastrophic backtracking. A crafted input can block the Node.js event loop for seconds or longer, resulting in a denial of service in build tools, CLI wrappers, and services that pass untrusted arguments to cross-spawn.
CVE-2024-38816spring-webmvc>=5.3.0 <5.3.40, >=6.0.0 <6.0.24, >=6.1.0 <6.1.13HighApplications serving static resources through RouterFunctions or WebMvc functional endpoints may be vulnerable to path traversal when a specially crafted URL is processed. An unauthenticated attacker can read files outside the configured resource directory if the application runs on a compatible servlet container and does not enforce additional path normalization.
CVE-2024-47554commons-io>=2.0 <2.18.0MediumThe XmlStreamReader implementation does not adequately limit resource consumption when parsing malicious XML input, allowing an attacker to trigger excessive memory allocation or CPU use. Applications that parse untrusted XML with commons-io may experience degraded performance or process termination; the update adds configurable limits and safer defaults for nested elements and attributes.
CVE-2024-45337golang.org/x/crypto/ssh>=0.0.0 <0.31.0HighApplications that use ServerConfig.PublicKeyCallback to make authorization decisions may be vulnerable to an authentication bypass when the callback returns an error after a successful key check. A remote client can exploit inconsistent callback behavior to authenticate without proper authorization; users should upgrade and review custom callback implementations for correct error handling.
table.brief: Security advisories: CVE ID / Package / Affected versions (ranges like >=2.0.0 <2.14.3) / Severity / Summary (long)

understanding.purpose: Help readers identify vulnerable dependencies, assess severity, and determine whether their installed versions are affected.
understanding.reading: Readers can scan CVE IDs, packages, and severity, then compare version ranges and read the relevant summary. Long summaries will often set row height, leaving room for version ranges to wrap within the same row.
groups: CVE ID and Package identify the advisory and dependency.
Affected versions and Package work together to determine exposure.
Severity and Summary convey urgency and describe the issue.
keep_intact: Individual version numbers and comparison operators
may_wrap: Affected version ranges at spaces or between comma-separated ranges

preferred.name: r3A
preferred.note: Give the summary 2px more than r2C while retaining enough room for the shown version ranges; check whether prose wrapping improves without splitting a range awkwardly.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Give versions 10px more than r0C to test a little more breathing room for the header and ranges, while retaining most of the improved summary measure.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Try a narrower version column and allow its header to wrap, giving the summary a wider measure. Check whether each complete version interval still reads cleanly on its own line.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Refine r1A by giving the summary 2px more while retaining nearly the same space for version pairs. Check whether the longer ranges still group cleanly.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Test a middle ground between r1A and r1B: give version ranges more room while recovering 5px for summaries. Check whether the header fits and whether the added range width changes the line breaks.

acceptable.name: r2C
acceptable.note: Move 6px from r1A's version column to the summary. Test whether the spring-webmvc bounds remain grouped more clearly than in r1C while the prose gains width.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Test the narrowest practical one-line versions header with slightly more summary space than r2B; check whether the compact header is worth the longer prose rows.

acceptable.name: r3C
acceptable.note: Explore a wider versions column to see whether multi-range entries become easier to compare, accepting narrower summaries and potentially taller rows.

bad.name: contrast
bad.note: The version column gains width that most entries cannot use, while the summaries become a narrow, heavily wrapped strip. The resulting taller rows make it harder to keep each advisory together while scanning.
bad.why: The version column gains width that most entries cannot use, while the summaries become a narrow, heavily wrapped strip. The resulting taller rows make it harder to keep each advisory together while scanning.

rationale: r3A keeps CVE IDs, package names and severity labels intact while giving the long summaries enough room to read comfortably. Its version ranges remain grouped by interval, including the three intervals for spring-webmvc. The two-line version header is a reasonable cost for the wider summary column.

general: Give identifiers enough width to stay intact and scannable.
Allocate width according to content and reading task; long prose benefits from more room than short categorical labels.
Judge wrapping by whether it preserves meaningful groups, not by line count alone.
specific: The longest package name uses essentially all of the 165px package column.
At 124px, the version column preserves the spring-webmvc intervals as three readable lines, while a narrower column in r1C breaks them across five.
A two-line Affected versions header frees space for summaries without obscuring the header.

tradeoffs: r3B and r2B keep every header on one line and preserve the version intervals, at the cost of narrower summaries and taller rows. A designer who prizes a compact header may prefer either.
uncertain: The ranges are conservative visual estimates, not browser-tested thresholds. They describe varying one column at a time while adjusting the others proportionally within the 792px budget; exact wrapping thresholds may differ by a pixel or two.

critique.good: Identifiers, package names, severity labels and headers remain intact. Most version ranges are easy to scan, and the table fits the viewport.
critique.problems: The summary is a narrow strip of short lines, producing very tall rows and large empty areas beneath the identifying fields. In the spring-webmvc row, a range is broken between its lower and upper bounds.
critique.cause: The 207px version column gives considerable space to mostly short values, leaving only 216px for the much longer summaries.

critique.good: The wider summary improves the reading rhythm and reduces row height. The spring-webmvc ranges sit on separate lines, while identifiers and package names remain intact.
critique.problems: The cross-spawn range breaks between its lower and upper bounds, making the second interval harder to read as a unit. Summaries still dominate tall rows with substantial empty space in the other columns.
critique.cause: The 165px version column fits more than one range fragment on the first line but not both complete cross-spawn ranges. The 258px summary column remains relatively narrow for the prose.

critique.good: The summary has the most comfortable measure of the three, and shorter rows bring each advisory's identifying information closer to the next. The cross-spawn and spring-webmvc ranges wrap into useful separate lines; names, identifiers and severity labels remain intact.
critique.problems: The affected-versions header is tight, and the version column has little room to accommodate longer individual ranges. The remaining row height is still driven by summaries, leaving broad empty areas under the short fields.
critique.cause: The 135px version column leaves 114px for text, while the fixed 131px and 165px identifier columns leave little spare width for further balancing.

critique.good: Identifiers, package names and severity labels stay intact. The longer version ranges generally form readable lines, and the summary has enough width for coherent prose.
critique.problems: The two-line version header makes the header row taller, while long summaries leave substantial empty space in the other columns.
critique.cause: The 132px version column is too narrow for its header on one line; the 291px summary column determines most row heights.

critique.good: All headers fit on one line, and the affected ranges remain easy to compare. Identifiers and package names stay intact.
critique.problems: The summaries are more cramped and produce taller rows, increasing the blank space beneath the shorter fields. The gain in version width does little for the displayed ranges.
critique.cause: Increasing the version column to 145px reduces the summary to 278px, even though the longest ranges still wrap.

critique.good: The wider summary improves prose rhythm and reduces the height of several rows. Identifiers, package names and severity labels remain intact.
critique.problems: The spring-webmvc range breaks across five lines, separating lower and upper bounds and placing parts of adjacent ranges together. This makes exposure harder to assess. The version header also wraps.
critique.cause: The 120px version column leaves only 99px for text, too little for some paired bounds.

critique.good: CVE IDs, package names and severity labels remain intact. Each version range wraps into readable units, and the row rules keep each advisory together.
critique.problems: The two-line Affected versions header makes the header band deeper than the other labels require. Summaries are narrow enough to create long rows and large empty areas in the identification columns.
critique.cause: The 130px versions column is too narrow for its header on one line, while the 293px summary column sets most row heights.

critique.good: All headers fit on one line, making the header band compact. Identifiers and package names remain intact, and the version ranges remain easy to associate with their packages.
critique.problems: The extra width in versions does not visibly reduce the wrapping of the multi-range entries. The narrower summaries produce longer rows, including an isolated final line in the commons-io summary.
critique.cause: Increasing versions to 140px leaves 283px for summaries; that width crosses a wrapping threshold without materially improving the displayed ranges.

critique.good: This is the strongest balance: the wider summaries read more comfortably and shorten several rows, while version ranges still wrap at sensible boundaries. Identifiers and package names remain intact.
critique.problems: The Affected versions header wraps, making the header band taller. The long summaries still leave substantial blank space under the short identification fields.
critique.cause: The 126px versions column cannot hold its header on one line. The 297px summary column necessarily governs row heights for this prose-heavy content.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r3A.why: CVE IDs and package names stay intact, version ranges mostly wrap at useful boundaries, and summaries have a comfortable measure. The affected-versions header wraps, and the long rows leave substantial white space in the shorter columns.

r1B.why: All headers fit on one line, identifiers stay intact, and version ranges are easy to scan. The slightly narrower summary column makes the prose and rows longer.

r1C.why: The summary has room to read, but the spring-webmvc version ranges break across five lines, separating bounds and making the ranges harder to compare.

contrast.why: Identifiers and headers fit, but the wide versions column leaves the summary cramped. Its short lines produce tall rows and large empty areas in the other columns.

ref_auto.why: The generous summary column reads well, but every CVE ID breaks across three lines and version bounds are heavily fragmented, hindering identification and comparison.

ref_equal.why: Near-equal columns squeeze the summaries into very short lines, creating extremely tall rows and vast empty areas. The long package name and callback identifier also break within their text.

raw.unsure: B's single-line header may be preferable if scanning column labels matters more than the wider summaries in A; both preserve the key identifiers and version ranges well.

r1C.why: CVE IDs and package names stay intact, and summaries have a useful measure. The narrow versions column breaks the spring-webmvc ranges across five lines, making them harder to compare.

ref_auto.why: The wide summary is comfortable to read, but every CVE ID is split across three lines and version ranges are heavily fragmented, weakening the table's key scanning fields.

r3A.why: CVE IDs and package names stay intact, version ranges wrap into readable groups, and the summary has enough width for comfortable reading. The rows remain easy to associate across columns.

contrast.why: Identifiers and version ranges scan well, but the narrow summary creates short lines and tall rows with large areas of empty space in the other columns.

ref_equal.why: Equal column widths leave the summary extremely narrow and create very tall rows. The long package name and callback identifier also break within their text.

r1B.why: Identifiers stay intact, the versions header fits on one line, and ranges group clearly. The summary is somewhat narrower, producing taller rows and occasional awkward breaks.

raw.unsure: C and F are close; the choice depends on whether a wider summary or a one-line versions header is more valuable to the reader.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
